12929-a-voyage-to-terra-australis-volume:
Matthew Flinders's Voyage to Terra Australis, volume one, records the survey of Australia's coasts in the early nineteenth century. Flinders notes in his preface that a book without an index deserved the pillory, so he gave each page a running title naming coast and anchorage instead. Charts, though absent from the text version, are cited throughout.

Coastal description fills the pages: beaches and rocky points rising to wooded tops, grassy hills behind Point Waterhouse, and soundings of eight down to four fathoms through a reef passage. Flinders writes as a careful seaman and surveyor. The volume stands as a founding record of Australian coastal exploration.
13121-a-voyage-to-terra-australis-volume:
Volume two of Matthew Flinders's Voyage to Terra Australis continues his survey of the Australian coasts in the Investigator. Flinders, who feared the pillory for a book without an index, gives careful logs, bearings, and notes on islands and reefs. The text keeps its charts by reference, though this plain-text copy lacks the charts themselves.

Entries record strong winds that barred landing, fires on Hammond's Island, and huts like sentry boxes on Wednesday Island. Later, Flinders leaves the Investigator for the Porpoise, carrying plants for Kew in a greenhouse on deck. The volume is a navigator's record, precise, daily, and full of the risks of mapping a new shore.
18135-dreamthorp:
Alexander Smith's book of essays takes its name from Dreamthorp, a small country village where the writer came to live. Smith says he was not born there, but settled there after trying other towns that pleased him less. The essays were issued in this series in 1905, with later reprints in 1907 and 1912.

The contents move from the village itself to wider subjects. Smith writes on the writing of essays, death and the fear of dying, William Dunbar, Geoffrey Chaucer, books and gardens, vagabonds, and Christmas. The tone is quiet and reflective. A reader gets country scenes mixed with short meditations on reading, memory, and common life.
36397-ruth-fielding-at-sunrise-farm-or-w:
Alice Emerson wrote a girls novel in the Ruth Fielding set, printed at New York in 1915. Ruth had starred in earlier books at a red mill, a snow camp, and a light house point. A front picture shows Ruth spotting Sadie Raby and crying out in surprise at the meeting.

Twenty five chapters open with sweet briars and sour pickles, then bring a wild girl and Sadie Rabys own tale. The Perkins folk, a tramp girl, and a trip toward Sunrise Farm fill the early run. Twins, a storm, a runaway, and a black horse raise the pace before the orphans luck is told near the close.
3711-the-relics-of-general-chasse-a-tale:
Anthony Trollope sets this comic tale in Antwerp just after Belgium won its freedom from Holland. The Dutch General Chasse had defended the citadel with gallantry, and English visitors flock to see what remains of his stand. Among them is the Reverend Augustus Horne, a hero worshipper who collects relics of the great man with pious zeal and shows them round as sacred scraps.

The joke turns when practical hands get hold of the treasures, since fine broadcloth proves too useful to stay in a shrine. Pieces meant for reverence end up measured for house slippers, and Horne's raptures meet the cool sense of Flemish housewives. The tale is brief and sly, a satire on souvenir hunting that still stings in an age of relics and autographs.
40229-history-of-randolph-macon-college-:
Richard Irby rescues college records in his History of Randolph-Macon College, Virginia, billed as the oldest incorporated Methodist college in America. A trustees' resolution, moved by J J Lafferty and W H Christian, serves as preface, thanking Irby for collecting material for a connected and authentic account. The history begins with early Methodist efforts to found schools.

Irby opens with John Wesley, educated at home and at Oxford, who founded the Kingswood School to join religion and learning. Bishop Asbury carried the same plans to America, where a postwar population of about three million was bent on restoring its wealth.
52303-the-history-of-lumsden-s-horse-a-c:
The History of Lumsden's Horse, edited by Pearse, a war correspondent, and published by Longmans in 1903, is the full record of a volunteer cavalry corps in the Boer War. The book follows the corps from its raising in India to its disbandment, with many portraits, pictures, and a map.

Chapters sail from Calcutta to Cape Town, ride to Bloemfontein, and take a baptism of fire at Ospruit. Prisoners, pursuits of De Wet, and the road to Pretoria fill the middle. Such unit histories, written close to the men, preserve the daily grain of a war that official reports smooth away.
55822-argonauts-of-the-western-pacific-a:
Argonauts of the Western Pacific is an anthropological study by Bronislaw Malinowski, published in 1922. Routledge issued it at London and Dutton at New York. Its subtitle promises native enterprise and adventure in Melanesian New Guinea. Five maps, sixty five illustrations, and two figures support the text. James George Frazer wrote the preface. Malinowski dedicates the book to Seligman, his friend and teacher.

Frazer praises both the method and the matter of the work. Malinowski had lived as a native among the natives for months together. In the Trobriand Islands he watched them daily at work and at play. He conversed with them in their own tongue, without interpreters. His earlier studies covered the family in Australia and the people of Mailu. The result, Frazer says, is a record of high scientific value. Social, religious, and economic life all come under his eye.
a-voyage-to-terra-australis-volume-1-und: Matthew Flinders voyages to Terra Australis in this first volume, undertaken to complete the discovery of that vast country in the years 1801, 1802, and 1803. The opening book treats his appointment to the Investigator, the outfit of the ship, instruments, books, and charts, presents for barter, and the officers and men of science who embarked. Departure from Spithead, variation of the compass, and the passage toward Port Jackson begin the circumnavigation.
a-voyage-to-terra-australis-volume-2-und: Matthew Flinders continues his voyage to Terra Australis in this second volume, carrying the story from the circumnavigation toward its troubled close. The third book opens with departure from Port Jackson in the Porpoise, accompanied by the Bridgewater and Cato, and the night shipwreck of Porpoise and Cato on a sand bank. From Wreck-Reef Bank through captivity to a prospect of liberty at Port Louis, the volume ends with arrival in England in 1810.
britannica-1911-aeolian-harp:
Aeolian Harp is an instrument article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The aeolian harp is a stringed instrument played by the wind itself. Its name comes from Aeolus, the god of the wind. No hands touch it; moving air sets the strings singing.

The entry describes how the instrument is built. A thin pine sound-box, about three feet long, carries a dozen or fewer gut strings. The strings differ in thickness but are tuned to the same note and left rather slack. They pass over two narrow bridges of hard wood. A raised board above them leaves a clear path for the breeze. The article names makers such as Kaufmann of Dresden who improved the design. Readers learn both the build of the harp and the secret of its soft, shifting tone.
britannica-1911-gould-benjamin-apthorp:
Benjamin Apthorp Gould (1824-1896) was an American astronomer born at Boston. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his Harvard study and training under Gauss at Göttingen. Coast survey work on longitude filled his early career back home. He helped fix longitude by telegraph and by Atlantic cable in 1866.

He founded the Astronomical Journal in 1849 and revived it later. In 1870 he began work at a new observatory at Cordoba in Argentina. Star catalogues from there listed tens of thousands of southern stars. Photo measures of the Pleiades made him a pioneer in that method. Late years went to southern star cluster plates at Cordoba.
britannica-1911-klerksdorp:
Klerksdorp is a short place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a town in the Transvaal region of South Africa. The town stands on the banks of a stream above where it joins the Vaal river. Rail lines link it to two larger towns in the region.

The entry gives the town count from the year nineteen hundred and four. It notes fine public buildings and rich ground nearby. Gold mines work close to the town, and coal and green gems are also found. A short history traces the first Boer village to eighteen thirty eight. The newer town across the stream dates from eighteen eighty eight.
britannica-1911-krugersdorp:
Krugersdorp is a town of the Transvaal, 21 miles N.W. of Johannesburg by rail. In 1904 it held 20,073 people, of whom 6946 were whites. It stands on the Witwatersrand, 5709 feet above the sea, and is a mining centre of some size. A railway starts here for Zeerust and Mafeking. The town was founded in 1887, when gold was found on the Rand, and is named after President Kruger.

Within the town stands the Paardekraal monument. It marks the Boer victory of 1838 over the Zulu king Dingaan, and Boers gather there each 16th of December. Here too, in December 1880, a great Boer meeting resolved to proclaim the Transvaal a free state once more. At Doornkop nearby, Dr Jameson and his raiders gave themselves up to Commandant Piet Cronje on the 2nd of January 1896.
britannica-1911-paley-frederick-apthorp:
Paley, Frederick Apthorp is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English classical scholar. Born at Easingwold in Yorkshire on the fourteenth of January 1815, he was the grandson of William Paley, the famous divine. He was educated at Shrewsbury school and at St John's College, Cambridge, taking his degree in 1838. He returned to Cambridge in 1860 as a coach.

The article lists his editions and his other post. In 1874 he became professor at the new Roman Catholic university at Kensington. His name rests on his editions of the Greek classics, Aeschylus above all. The article adds that he knew building well too, and published manuals of Gothic architecture and of Gothic mouldings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antwerp:
Antwerp, the Belgian city on the Scheldt is treated here through its long political, commercial, and church history. Its people were certainly Christian from about the midpoint of the seventh century, and saints such as Dymphna, Eligius, Amandus, and Willibrord figure in its early story. Pillaged by Northmen in 835, it rose again and became capital of the Margraves of Antwerp in the tenth and eleventh centuries. It won privileges from the dukes of Brabant in the thirteenth and fourteenth.

Counts of Flanders then held it as lords, and in the fifteenth century it passed under Burgundy, through which it rose to its highest point. The article moves from origins and early bishops to trade, rule, and religious life, giving a city biography rather than a travel sketch. Readers tracing the Low Countries will find Antwerp placed at the meeting point of river trade, princely power, and Catholic tradition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-herp:
Henry Herp, a Franciscan of the Strict Observance in the fifteenth century, also called Harp, is known only from the last thirty years of his life. Born at Düren or nearby, he served as rector of the Brethren of the Common Life at Delft and Gouda. He took the Franciscan habit at Ara Coeli in Rome during a pilgrimage in 1450, became provincial of Cologne from 1470 to 1473, and died as guardian of Mechlin in 1478.

Only one work appeared in his lifetime, the Speculum Aureum of 1474, with 213 sermons on the Commandments for preachers and confessors, later joined by a further 222 sermons. His mystical writings, above all the Theologica Mystica written on Mount Alverno, circulated widely in Flemish, Latin, French, and German. A 1556 edition was censured by the Index and corrected editions followed. The Franciscan chapter of Toledo recommended his works in 1663 as standard writings in mystical theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jakob-middend:
Theologian and historian Jakob Middendorp was born about 1537 at Oldenzaal, or by other accounts at Ootmarsum in Overijssel. He died at Cologne on 13 January 1611. He called himself Otmersensis on his work De celebrioribus Academiis. He studied humanities at Zwolle's Fraterherren gymnasium. He studied philosophy and law at Cologne university. There he became doctor of philosophy and both laws, and licentiate of theology. He also taught peripatetic philosophy at the Montanum gymnasium.

He stayed in Westphalia during troubles in Cologne archdiocese under Archbishop Gebhard Truchsess von Waldburg. He taught at various foreign academies. Later he returned to Cologne and spent most of his life there. In 1580 he became dean of St Maria ad gradus. In 1596 he became dean of St Andreas. In 1601 he became canon of the cathedral chapter. He later served as rector of Cologne university. The entry presents a wandering scholar settled into Cologne offices.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melchior-hitt:
Melchior Hittorp, a theologian and writer on the liturgy, was born at Cologne about 1525 and died there in 1584. Once his studies were done he took the licentiate in theology and became a canon at St. Maria ad Gradus. Jacob Pamelius asked him for the book: Pamelius was then a canon at Bruges and later became Bishop of St-Omer. Hittorp brought out in 1568 a volume of old fathers' writings on the Church's divine offices.

The book pulls together pieces by Isidore of Seville, Alcuin, Rhabanus Maurus, Strabo, Berno, and others on Catholic worship. Ferrari put out a fuller edition in 1591, and Paris reprinted it in the Magna Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum in 1644. The sketch is brief and leans on Hurter, the Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie, and Harzheim, and it shows Hittorp as a collector who kept early liturgical texts safe for later scholars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-polycarp:
Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna and martyr about 155, links the apostles to the second-century Church. Born about 69, he knew John, taught Irenaeus, and wrote an Epistle to the Philippians answering their requests for exhortation, a letter to Antioch, and any epistles of Ignatius he held. Ignatius wrote him an epistle of his own from Smyrna.

The Letter of the Smyrnaeans recounts his martyrdom: arrested in old age, he refused to revile Christ, was burned at the stake, and was finished with a dagger when fire failed. His feast and his stand against Marcion and the Gnostics anchor the entry. Readers find sources weighed with care, from Ignatius and Irenaeus to the martyrdom narrative itself.
dreamthorp:
Alexander Smith, a Scottish poet and essayist, wrote the essays of Dreamthorp in a village he declines to place on any map. In the title essay he tells how he came to the place one summer evening. Sunset lit the westward windows. Children played in one straggling street, and a ruined castle tower rose full of swallows. He took off his knapsack there for good.

The set ranges widely. Titles promise pieces on the writing of essays, on death and the fear of dying, and on Dunbar and Chaucer. Others treat books and gardens, and vagabonds. In Men of Letters he notes that writers come from the stray talent of the world. Doctors, lawyers, clergymen, and Bohemians all drift in. Smith's voice is quiet and bookish. The village frame lets each essay feel like a walk and a talk.
the-relics-of-general-chasse-a-tale-of-a:
Anthony Trollope's tale, transcribed from an 1864 Chapman and Hall collection, recalls when Belgium was still Flanders and Brabant under Holland and won independence by revolution. Its key military episode was the siege of Antwerp, defended gallantly but in vain by Dutch General Chasse.

Afterward Antwerp drew visitors eager to praise the general and view the remains of his defense, among them two Englishmen. The hero, the Reverend Augustus Horne, is a beneficed clergyman full of quiet mirth and polished wit who has known no care or sorrow. A relic hunt with such a hero promises comedy edged with sentiment.
